newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Japan revises NTT law, readies for Big Bang.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Japan revises NTT law, readies for Big Bang.

text.p: Japan on Friday changed its telecom laws, including one governing Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), in preparation for "Big Bang" reforms in the nation's lucrative telecommunications sector.

The Upper House of parliament passed a law to allow the telecoms giant to be split up into three units under a single holding firm, paving the way for the telecoms titan to realise its long-held dream of entering the global market.

"The revision will make it possible for Japanese telecom firms to survive severe competition either by themselves or through tie-up with other firms," Posts and Telecommunications Minister Hisao Horinouchi said in a statement.

The deregulation will activate the businesses of Japanese and foreign telecom operators, which should in turn benefit Japanese consumers in the way of diversified services and lower prices, the minister said.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced his Big Bang reform plan last November to make domestic markets "free, fair and global" and compete more effectively against New York and London.

Before the revision, the NTT law had stipulated that the company, two-thirds owned by the government, must limit its operations to the domestic market. The firm dominates Japan's domestic phone networks, with an 80 percent market share.

"The revision will make it possible for us to enter the international telecoms business. Now we are ready for globalisation and the multimedia business," NTT president Junichiro Miyazu told a news conference.

Under the planned restructuring, NTT will be split into two regional local carriers and one long-distance group under a holding company. NTT is mapping out details of the plan and is likely to implement the changes as early as 1999.
"The restructuring will be implemented soon after we get approval at the annual shareholders' meeting in 1999," Miyazu said.
Miyazu said NTT intends to seek government approval for a unit to offer international call services after the revised telecom bill takes effect in about several weeks.

Earlier this week, NTT said that it would form a unit, possibly as soon as July, to start international services in autumn. NTT plans to provide Japanese multinationals abroad with information and systems integration services.
The telecom giant also plans to seek telecommunications licences in Europe, Asia and the United States in order to provide the companies with voice and data services.
The revision of other telecom laws on Friday also opened the door for Japan's largest international telecoms firm, Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd (KDD) to offer domestic phone services.
"We would like to offer high-quality, low-priced comprehensive domestic and international services as soon as possible," KDD president Tadashi Nishimoto said in a statement.

Earlier this year, KDD said it planned to boost investment in foreign markets over the next five years, launch a domestic phone service in July and speed up a rationalisation programme, spurred into action by NTT's push into the international arena.
